conditions: Stage IV melanoma patients receiving ICI
external_ask: 搜索并识别在ICI治疗实体瘤患者中，直接比较不同抗生素类别（如β-内酰胺类、氟喹诺酮类、糖肽类）对OS或PFS影响的前瞻性研究或汇总分析。重点关注是否有研究报道了类别间差异的统计显著性，以及是否存在一致的‘安全’类别证据。
limits: 需要寻找至少一项前瞻性比较研究或大型汇总分析（pooled analysis），直接比较不同抗生素类别（如β-内酰胺类 vs. 氟喹诺酮类 vs. 糖肽类）在ICI治疗实体瘤患者中的OS或PFS差异，并提供明确的统计显著性结果。目前的材料仅为回顾性单中心研究，且结果存在异质性，不足以回答关于“统计学显著差异”的确切问题，也无法排除混杂因素。
question: Do prospective comparative studies or pooled analyses in ICI-treated solid tumor patients demonstrate statistically significant differences in overall survival or progression-free survival between specific antibiotic classes (e.g., beta-lactams vs. fluoroquinolones vs. glycopeptides)?
read_focus: 重点检索涉及ICI治疗实体瘤的前瞻性临床试验亚组分析，或包含多个中心的大型回顾性队列研究的汇总分析，特别关注是否进行了抗生素类别间的头对头比较（head-to-head comparison）。

usable_content: This study conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 48 studies (12,794 patients) evaluating the association between antibiotic use and clinical outcomes in cancer patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). The authors reported that antibiotic use was associated with shorter overall survival (HR 1.88; 95% C.I. 1.59-2.22) and progression-free survival (HR 1.52; 95% C.I. 1.36-1.70). Subgroup analysis indicated the negative association with progression-free survival was stronger in renal cell carcinoma or melanoma than lung cancer. The authors noted substantial heterogeneity for all outcomes and found that only antibiotic administration >1 month prior to ICI initiation was associated with increased disease progression. This study conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 41 studies (10,857 patients) evaluating the association between antibiotic use and clinical outcomes in cancer patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). The authors found that overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were shorter, and response rates lower, in patients receiving antibiotics compared to those who did not, both in univariate and adjusted analyses. The study concluded that there is a significant association between antibiotic use and unfavorable clinical outcomes. Crucially for the gap, the authors noted significant heterogeneity across outcomes and explicitly stated that this underscores the need for more detailed studies with stratification by 'antibacterial' factors, implying that the current pooled evidence primarily supports a broad antibiotic effect rather than class-specific distinctions. This systematic review and meta-analysis explicitly addresses the gap by stating that class-specific antibiotic comparisons could not be performed due to heterogeneity in ABT definitions, exposure windows, and limited reporting of ABT classes across the 15 included studies (52,489 patients). The authors report: 'heterogeneity in ABT definitions, exposure windows, and reporting of ABT classes limited our ability to perform detailed class-specific or dose-dependent analyses.' Table 3 shows that many studies did not report specific antibiotic classes (marked 'NR'). The meta-analysis compared ABT exposure versus no ABT exposure only, finding ABT associated with worse OS (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.03–1.29) and a trend toward worse PFS (HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.95–1.27). When antibiotic classes were reported, exposure predominantly involved broad-spectrum agents (beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, etc.) without head-to-head comparisons between classes. This satisfies the second success criterion: a clear statement from a systematic review that existing evidence only supports broad-spectrum antibiotic overall effects without class-specific differentiation.
